passage: Daycare note, Tuesday, from Ganga. Joseph (20 months) spent a long time at the snack table today. He picked up single puffed-rice grains between thumb and first finger, one at a time, and ate every one. With the spoon he scooped dal, turned it halfway to his mouth, and most of it landed on his bib. He tried again without fuss. At block time his tower reached three before it fell. Next I'll put out thicker crayons and a bowl with a curved edge for scooping. 🙂

qa.q: How many blocks high did Joseph's tower get?
qa.a: Three blocks before it fell.

qa.q: What does Joseph trying the spoon again without fuss suggest about his mood?
qa.a: He seemed calm and interested, more keen to keep practising than upset by the spill.

qa.q: Why might Ganga's plan for a curved bowl help Joseph?
qa.a: A curved edge makes it easier to push food onto the spoon, so he can succeed more often while practising.

qa.q: What might Joseph's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would probably feel pleased to hear his finger skills are growing, and less bothered by a messy bib. 😊

grounding: Shows a toddler's small finger movements: picking up grains, using a spoon and building a tower.

passage: In the courtyard, Urmila shells peas into a steel plate while her granddaughter Gurpreet, almost two, squats beside her. Gurpreet pinches one green pea between two fingers, lifts it high, and drops it into the plate with a clink. She laughs and does it again, and again. When a pod won't open, she hands it up to her grandmother and waits, palm flat, for the peas to be tipped in. By the time the plate is full, a little heap of it came from her small fingers.

qa.q: What sound does the pea make when Gurpreet drops it?
qa.a: A clink in the steel plate.

qa.q: Why does Gurpreet keep dropping peas again and again?
qa.a: She seems to enjoy the clink and the success of picking each pea up, so she wants to repeat it.

qa.q: How could Urmila keep this practice going safely?
qa.a: She can keep giving Gurpreet things to pick up and sort while sitting close and watching, since small items can go into mouths.

qa.q: What is it like for Urmila to have Gurpreet helping?
qa.a: The work is slower, but she gets company and sees her granddaughter's fingers getting surer.

grounding: Shows a toddler using a pinch grip with peas during an ordinary village chore.

passage: Marek, two, sits on the kitchen floor of the flat in Krakow with a set of plastic cups. Fatima, his mother, is peeling potatoes. He sets the big cup down, then the middle one, lining up the edges with his tongue poking out. The smallest cup slips twice. The third time he pinches it by the rim and places it on top, then claps and looks up at her. "Tower!" he says. She claps back, and he knocks it down to start over.

qa.q: What was Fatima doing while Marek played?
qa.a: She was peeling potatoes.

qa.q: What does Marek's tongue poking out suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was concentrating hard and felt determined to line up the cups, and his clapping at the end shows he felt proud.

qa.q: How could Fatima support Marek's finger control next?
qa.a: She could offer other things to stack or pinch, like large pegs or wooden rings, and let him keep trying without doing it for him.

qa.q: If you were Fatima, what would you want Marek to feel from your clapping?
qa.a: I'd want him to feel his effort was noticed and shared, so he keeps trying tricky things.

grounding: Shows a toddler refining grip and placement while stacking cups.

passage: I'm Nilesh, and I sit next to Ojas's highchair at family dinners. At first, Ojas, fifteen months, grabbed rice with his whole fist and most of it fell. Tonight I watched him pick up single peas between his thumb and one finger, slowly, tongue poking out. He dropped one, frowned, and picked it up again. Then he tried his spoon. It tipped halfway. He banged it on the tray and tried once more.

qa.q: How did Ojas pick up the peas tonight?
qa.a: He picked them up between his thumb and one finger.

qa.q: What might Ojas's frown after dropping a pea suggest?
qa.a: It might suggest he was a little frustrated, though he kept trying.

qa.q: How could the family support Ojas's small hand skills?
qa.a: They could keep giving him small, safe finger foods and let him try the spoon without rushing to help.

qa.q: How does Nilesh see Ojas's progress?
qa.a: Nilesh notices the change from grabbing with a whole fist to picking single peas carefully.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing a toddler refining a pincer grasp and trying to use a spoon.

passage:
Monday: Damini, one and a half, knocks over the three wooden blocks her uncle Mridul builds, and laughs.

Wednesday: She puts one block on top of another. It wobbles and falls. She pushes it away.

Saturday: Mridul holds the bottom block still. Damini sets two blocks on top, slowly, pressing each one down with her fingers. The tower stands. She claps and looks at Mridul, then points for more.

qa.q: How many blocks did Damini set on top on Saturday?
qa.a: She set two blocks on top.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when she pushed the blocks away on Wednesday?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated when her block wobbled and fell.

qa.q: What small step did Mridul take that helped Damini?
qa.a: He held the bottom block still, making it easier for her to stack.

qa.q: What would change if Mridul had built the tower for her every time?
qa.a: Damini would have fewer chances to practise stacking and might not learn it as quickly.

grounding: Shows a toddler's fine motor skill for stacking blocks growing over several days.

passage: Saurabh put a small heap of boiled peas on the steel plate and waited. His son Deepak, eighteen months old, first slapped the heap with his whole palm, and peas flew under the sofa. Then he stopped, pinched one pea between his thumb and one finger, and carried it slowly to his mouth. He chewed, looked at his father, and reached for another. Twenty minutes later the peas were gone, and so was Saurabh's plan to finish lunch quickly.

qa.q: What did Saurabh put on the steel plate?
qa.a: A small heap of boiled peas.

qa.q: What does Deepak looking at his father after the first pea suggest?
qa.a: He seemed pleased with himself and maybe wanted Saurabh to notice his new trick.

qa.q: What could Saurabh try at the next meal to help Deepak practise?
qa.a: Offer small soft pieces again and plan extra time, since picking them up one by one is slow but good practice.

qa.q: What would change if Saurabh had fed Deepak with a spoon to save time?
qa.a: Lunch would be faster, but Deepak would lose the chance to practise his thumb-and-finger pinch.

grounding: Shows a toddler moving from a whole-hand slap to a careful finger pinch while feeding himself.

passage:
"Jatin, give me the spoon," said Karthik, his big brother. "You're making a mess."
"No! Me!" Jatin gripped the spoon in his fist and plunged it into the curd rice.
"Amma, he's dropping more than he eats."
"Look how he's holding it now," Amma said from the stove. "Fingers, not the whole fist."
Jatin turned the spoon; half the rice fell, and the rest reached his mouth.
"He got it!" Karthik said. "Okay, okay. I'll hold the bowl still."
"Good idea," said Amma.

qa.q: What was Jatin eating?
qa.a: Curd rice.

qa.q: Why did Jatin shout "No! Me!" when Karthik asked for the spoon?
qa.a: He wanted to feed himself and felt determined, maybe cross, at the idea of his brother taking over.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Karthik holding the bowl still worked, because it helped Jatin keep practising instead of taking the spoon away.

qa.q: How does Karthik's view of Jatin change during the meal?
qa.a: He starts out annoyed by the mess, then cheers when Jatin succeeds and decides to help.

grounding: Shows a toddler refining his grip on a spoon while family members respond to the mess and the progress.

passage:
Note from Sonali, room teacher, 22 December
Today we made paper stars for the Christmas tree. Jaya stacked the wooden blocks into a tower of five before it fell, and she clapped. At the craft table she picked up sequins one at a time with her thumb and finger and pressed each onto the glue. When one stuck to her finger she shook her hand hard and frowned. I showed her how to wipe it on the paper, and she tried it twice. Tomorrow I'll put out bigger beads for threading 🙂

qa.q: How many blocks were in Jaya's tower before it fell?
qa.a: Five blocks were in the tower before it fell.

qa.q: What does Jaya's frown suggest when the sequin stuck to her finger?
qa.a: She seemed frustrated that the sequin wouldn't let go, since her careful pinching had stopped working.

qa.q: Why is Sonali's plan for bigger beads a good next step?
qa.a: It builds on the pinching Jaya is already doing and gives her a new task that is a little harder but still manageable.

qa.q: How might Jaya's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would likely feel proud and pleased to see her small hand skills described in such detail.

grounding: Shows a toddler using a finger pinch and stacking blocks, noted by a teacher who plans the next step.

passage: Before Dussehra, Tanuja sat in the courtyard of their village house threading marigold garlands. Mridul, fifteen months, sat beside the heap of flowers. He pinched one orange marigold between finger and thumb, stared at it, and dropped it into her brass plate. Plop. He did it again, tongue poking out. Tanuja nudged the plate a little further away. Mridul shuffled, pinched, reached, plopped, and clapped his hands.

qa.q: Where did Mridul drop the flowers?
qa.a: Into her brass plate.

qa.q: What does Mridul's tongue poking out suggest?
qa.a: Mridul was concentrating hard, absorbed and pleased with the game.

qa.q: How did Tanuja make the task a little harder in a good way?
qa.a: She nudged the plate further away, so Mridul had to reach, pinch and aim, building finger control.

qa.q: How might Tanuja feel watching him?
qa.a: Tanuja probably feels amused and proud, seeing him practise such a careful grasp while she works.

grounding: In a village courtyard before Dussehra, a toddler practises pinching and placing marigolds.

passage: On Christmas Eve in Uppsala, the kitchen smelled of rice porridge and cinnamon. Santiago, twenty months, refused to be fed. "Me!" He gripped the spoon in his fist, scooped, tipped half onto the table, and got the rest into his mouth. His mother, Ingrid, didn't wipe anything. She gently turned his wrist so the spoon stayed flat. On the next scoop, most of it arrived. Santiago banged the spoon on the bowl, beaming, porridge on his nose.

qa.q: What did the kitchen smell of on Christmas Eve?
qa.a: Rice porridge and cinnamon.

qa.q: How did Santiago feel when most of the porridge reached his mouth?
qa.a: Santiago felt proud and happy, banging the spoon and beaming.

qa.q: What small help did Ingrid give, and why was it useful?
qa.a: She turned his wrist so the spoon stayed flat, helping him succeed while still feeding himself.

qa.q: How might Ingrid see the spilled porridge?
qa.a: Ingrid sees the mess as part of learning, not a problem, so she lets Santiago keep trying.

grounding: On Christmas Eve in Sweden, a toddler insists on using a spoon himself and his mother gives a small assist.

passage: I'm Omkar, Charu's big brother. In May it was too hot to go out, so after lunch we stayed under the fan with my wooden blocks. Charu is two. At first she only knocked my towers down. Then one afternoon she put one block on another, holding her breath. Then a third. It fell. She looked at me like she might cry, then picked the block up again. Four stayed up. She clapped so hard she knocked them down herself.

qa.q: When did they play with the blocks?
qa.a: After lunch in May, under the fan.

qa.q: What might Charu have felt when the third block fell?
qa.a: Charu seemed upset and close to crying, but determined enough to try again.

qa.q: How could Omkar support Charu's stacking?
qa.a: He could offer big, easy blocks, cheer her tries, and let her build without taking over.

qa.q: How does Omkar see Charu's progress?
qa.a: Omkar watches closely and seems proud, noticing how she went from knocking towers down to stacking four.

grounding: A big brother describes his toddler sister learning to stack blocks during hot summer afternoons.

passage:
Monday before Diwali: Gargi sits in a heap of puffed rice on the kitchen floor, scooping it with her whole fist. Most falls out.

Thursday: Raghav notices her picking up single grains with her thumb and first finger, one at a time, and dropping them into a steel bowl.

Diwali night: she carries the bowl to the rangoli, carefully places three grains in the middle, and looks up at Raghav, beaming.

qa.q: What did Gargi drop the grains into on Thursday?
qa.a: She dropped them into a steel bowl.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel when she placed the grains in the rangoli?
qa.a: Gargi seemed proud and pleased, beaming up at Raghav.

qa.q: How could Raghav keep supporting Gargi's fine motor skills during the festival?
qa.a: Give her more safe, small things to pick up and place, like puffed rice or flower petals, while he watches.

qa.q: What was it like for Raghav to watch Gargi over the week?
qa.a: Raghav was likely delighted to see her move from fistfuls to careful single grains.

grounding: Over a Diwali week, a toddler moves from whole-hand scooping to a pincer grasp for small grains.

passage:
It was mango season, and the Mumbai flat smelt of it. Vidya Nani put a small bowl of mango pulp in front of Arohi and handed her a spoon.

Arohi held it in her fist. The first scoop went to her cheek. The second went to her nose. Nani wiped nothing.

On the fifth try, the spoon went into her mouth. Arohi stopped, surprised, then banged the spoon on the tray and went for more.

qa.q: What did Nani put in front of Arohi?
qa.a: She put a small bowl of mango pulp.

qa.q: What did Arohi feel when the spoon finally reached her mouth?
qa.a: Arohi seemed surprised and then excited, banging the spoon and going for more.

qa.q: What did Vidya Nani do that helped Arohi learn to use the spoon?
qa.a: She let Arohi try again and again without wiping or taking over, so Arohi could practise.

qa.q: How might Nani feel about the messy mango pulp everywhere?
qa.a: Nani seems relaxed and patient, happy to accept the mess for the sake of Arohi's learning.

grounding: A toddler learns to hold a spoon and feed herself mango pulp during summer, refining small muscle control.

passage:
"Look, Amandeep. She's stacking," Rehana whispered.

Noor, sitting under the Christmas tree in their Chandigarh flat, put one red block on another.

"Two!" said Amandeep. "Last week she only knocked them down."

Noor added a third. It wobbled. She pressed it gently with her palm.

"She's steadying it," Rehana said.

A fourth block. The tower fell. Noor looked at the pile, then started again.

qa.q: Where was Noor sitting?
qa.a: Noor was sitting under the Christmas tree in their Chandigarh flat.

qa.q: How did Noor seem to feel when the tower fell?
qa.a: Noor seemed calm and determined rather than upset, because she looked at the pile and started again.

qa.q: How can Rehana and Amandeep support Noor's stacking?
qa.a: Give her more time with blocks, cheer her attempts, and let her rebuild on her own.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel seeing Noor stack two blocks?
qa.a: Amandeep was excited and proud, since last week she only knocked them down.

grounding: During the Christmas season, a toddler begins stacking and steadying blocks, refining fine motor control.

passage:
Crèche note, Tuesday
Deepak ate his dal-rice with the spoon today and only needed help with the last few bites. At snack time he picked up single peas between thumb and finger, very slowly, and posted them into his mouth. His cousin Lalit, from the older group, built him a tower of three blocks. Deepak added a fourth, then knocked it all down, squealing. Lalit groaned, then built it again. Tomorrow I'll put out the big wooden beads for threading. 🙂
Ms Anjali

qa.q: What did Deepak pick up between thumb and finger at snack time?
qa.a: He picked up single peas between thumb and finger.

qa.q: What does Deepak's squeal suggest about how he felt about the tower?
qa.a: He added a fourth block, knocked it all down and squealed, which shows he felt delighted and excited.

qa.q: What small step would help Deepak keep practising with his fingers at home?
qa.a: His family could offer small, soft finger foods and let him feed himself, even if it's slow and messy.

qa.q: What is it like for Lalit when Deepak knocks the tower down?
qa.a: Lalit is a bit fed up at first and groans, but still cares enough to build it again for a younger cousin.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler refining small hand movements: using a spoon, picking up peas with thumb and finger, and stacking blocks.
